title: Animals 1

subtitle.text: The rat smells the cheese on the table.
He will eat it in his hole.
The dog buries the bone in the yard.
He will eat it later.
The bird pulls the worm from the ground.
She will feed it to her babies.
The rabbit pulls the carrot from the ground.
He will share it with his friend.
The squirrel stores the nuts in the trunk.
She will eat them this winter.
The bear catches the fish in the stream.
She will take them to her cub.
The frog eats the fly in the air.
The frog is still hungry.
Yummy!
What will you eat now?
Many different animals lay eggs.
Baby animals grow inside them.
One day the eggs will hatch.
What animals will come out of them?
These eggs rest in sand.
The eggs are very soft.
One night they hatch.
The animals are sea turtles!
The sea turtles crawl across the beach.
They swim away in the ocean.
These eggs sit in a nest.
The eggs have a smooth, hard shell.
[i@Crack!@i]
Owlets poke out their heads!
The parents feed them worms.
One day the owlets fly away!
These tiny eggs float in a pond.
Jelly covers the eggs.
One day they hatch into tadpoles.
Soon tiny legs grow.
The tadpoles' tails shrink.
They are frogs now!
These tiny eggs stick to a leaf.
Caterpillars hatch from the eggs.
The caterpillars eat leaves and grow.
Then their bodies become hard.
They don't move for two weeks.
Finally, beautiful butterflies pop out!
Many different animals hatch from eggs.
Which one is your favorite?
"Good morning, class," Mr. Zimmer said.
[s@"Good morning, class," Mr. Zimmer said.
"Ready for our zoo tour?"
"Yes!" called the kids.
"I hope we see cheetahs!" Rosa thought.
"Today we will visit animals with something in common," said Mr. Zimmer.
"These animals use their colors or patterns to hide.
This is called camouflage."
"You mean like military clothing?" Frank asked.
"Yes," said Mr. Zimmer.
"Camouflage clothing protects soldiers.
They can blend in with their surroundings.
Animals use camouflage for protection too."
The class walked to a hut.
A sign read Reptiles and Amphibians.
"Many reptiles use camouflage to hide from their enemies.
Look at this lizard," Mr. Zimmer said.
It was hard to see the lizard.
Its skin was the same color as the rock.
"Mr. Zimmer?" Rosa asked.
"Can camouflage help animals hunt too?"
"That's a great question, Rosa!" Mr. Zimmer said.
He pointed to a bullfrog.
"This bullfrog uses color to hide while it waits for food.
It is the same color as grass and leaves."
"It can trick its prey!" said Olivia.
"Where are we going next?" Frank asked.
"To see the owls," Mr. Zimmer said.
The class stopped in front of the Owl House.
"Where are they?" Olivia asked.
"Owls use pattern camouflage," Mr. Zimmer said.
"See if you can find one."
Rosa looked closely at the tree.
"I see an owl!" she said.
"Its feathers are the same pattern as tree bark!"
"Right. The cheetahs are next," said Mr. Zimmer.
"Yes!" cried Rosa.
The class walked to a large grassy area.
Rosa looked at the cheetahs' spots.
"How are cheetah spots camouflage?"
"Well," said Mr. Zimmer.
"The spots help cheetahs blend in with shadows in the grass.
This helps cheetahs when they hunt.
And it keeps cheetah cubs safe from other big cats."
"That's cool!" said Rosa.
Rosa looked at the pattern on Frank's shirt.
He was leaning against a brick wall.
"Look!" Rosa said.
"Frank is using camouflage too!"
Hank was hiking in the woods with his mom and his sister.
Their dog, Sadie, was trotting beside them.
Suddenly Sadie spotted a skunk.
"Sadie, no!" Mom shouted as Sadie bolted toward it.
But Sadie didn't listen.
The skunk raised its tail.
Sadie yelped and ran back to them.
Her eyes were watering, and she stunk!
"Oh no," Ella said.
"Sadie got sprayed!"
They went home to give the dog a bath.
"Skunks are mean!" Hank said as Mom turned on the hose.
Mom shrugged. "That skunk was just defending itself."
"That's right," Ella said.
"Most animals have to protect themselves.
Otherwise, predators will eat them."
"But rabbits don't spray Sadie," Hank said.
"And she chases them."
"Rabbits have a different way to defend themselves," Ella said.
"They run fast and then hide.
Their speed helps them escape danger."
Mom scrubbed Sadie. "Can you two think of other ways animals defend themselves?"
Hank thought for a moment. "I know! Porcupines shoot quills!"
Ella laughed. "Porcupines don't actually shoot quills.
But their quills do break off when they're attacked.
The quills are really sharp.
They stick into the predator's skin."
"That reminds me of another animal defense," Hank said.
"Last year I learned about lizards that make their tails fall off."
Mom looked curious. "How is that self-defense?"
Hank smiled. "A predator that's chasing a lizard will likely grab the lizard's tail.
So, the lizard lets it fall off and then hurries away."
"I just thought of an animal that moves slowly," Ella said.
"And it doesn't have anything sharp like quills.
But it can still protect itself."
Hank scratched his head. "What is it?"
Ella grinned. "A turtle! Its shell is like a suit of armor!"
"I love turtles," Hank said.
"But I almost stepped on one the other day.
It blended in with the leaves."
"So turtles have two kinds of self-defense," Mom said.
"They have armor and camouflage to blend in."
"Some animals protect themselves by not blending in at all," Ella said.
"Really?" Hank asked.
Ella nodded. "Poison frogs are bright and colorful.
But those pretty colors are a warning.
They tell predators, if you eat me, you'll probably die.
That's because their skin has deadly, toxic chemicals."
Mom rinsed the soapy water off Sadie.
The dog shivered and hung her head.
"Poor Sadie looks so unhappy." Hank chuckled.
"I bet she wishes she could defend herself from baths!"
Some of my friends have dogs that work.
My friend Susie cannot see.
Her dog walks to school. Good dog!
My friend Tim cannot walk.
His dog gets the mail. Good dog!
My friend Ann cannot hear.
Her dog hears someone knocking. Good dog!
My friend Mr. Jones is a police officer.
His dog catches criminals. Good dog!
My friend Miss Sanchez is a soldier.
Her dog guards the gate. Good dog!
My friend Mrs. Kim works at the airport.
Her dog looks for drugs and bombs. Good dog!
My friend Mr. Wilson is a dogsled racer.
His dogs pull the sled. Good dogs!
I like my friends. I like their dogs too!
Who makes honey?
Honeybees do, of course!
But making honey is a special job for worker honeybees.
How do these bees make honey?
They do it together!
Older worker bees leave the hive early in the morning.
Their job is to gather nectar from flowers.
They suck the nectar with their long, straw-like tongues.
Then they store it in their honey stomachs.
Honeybees have two stomachs.
The normal stomach digests food.
But the honey stomach is just for storing nectar.
This special stomach can hold a lot of nectar!
Filling a honey stomach isn't an easy job.
Bees must visit hundreds of flowers.
That's a lot of flying!
After the bees fill their honey stomachs, they return to the hive.
There, they pass the nectar to other worker bees.
The new workers put the nectar inside the honeycomb.
Honeycomb is a group of small cells inside the hive.
Then worker bees fan the nectar with their wings.
This dries it. Slowly, it grows thick.
The thick, sweet liquid is now honey!
The honey is an important food for the bees.
They store extra honey in the honeycomb.
They will eat it in the winter.
Making honey is hard work.
The worker bees do it together—like a team.
Dan and Jan were at the natural history museum.
They walked into a dark room.
"I wonder what's in here," said Jan.
A screen flashed on.
"I am the Book of Tails, or BOT," said a voice.
"Whoa," said Dan and Jan.
"Choose an animal to learn about its tail," said BOT.
Dan touched the Dolphin button.
"Dolphin," said BOT.
"A dolphin moves its tail up and down.
This helps it move forward in the water.
A whale does the same."
"Like a fish," said Dan.
"Not exactly," said BOT.
"A fish moves its tail from side to side."
"This is fun!" said Jan. "Let me try!"
"Zebra. A zebra flicks away flies with its tail.
A cow and a horse do this too."
"Alligator. An alligator attacks enemies with its tail.
Its tail is thick and strong."
"Kangaroo. A kangaroo has a long and strong tail.
It uses its tail to sit up.
It also uses its tail to walk."
"I never knew that," said Dan. "It's my turn again."
"Chameleon. A chameleon is special because it changes colors.
A chameleon's tail is special too.
It helps a chameleon balance on branches."
"Dog. A dog wags its tail to say hello.
This shows that it is excited."
"Dan! Jan!" called a voice from outside the room.
"That's Mom," said Jan.
"We have to go," said Dan.
He touched the Exit button.
"Thank you for visiting," said BOT.
"Come back again to learn more."
"We will," said Dan and Jan. "Bye!"
A young gazelle walked across the savanna.
He ate some grass and a few leaves.
The sun felt very hot.
"I'm thirsty," said the gazelle.
"I'll go to the water hole."
When the gazelle reached the water hole, he took a few sips.
Then he looked up.
Another young animal was watching the gazelle.
The animal had sharp teeth and claws.
But he didn't look mean.
The two animals playfully chased each other.
They splashed in the water.
When the sun began to set, the gazelle headed home.
He told his mother about his new friend.
"What did he look like?" she asked.
The gazelle told her.
"He's a lion!" she said.
"You can't be friends with him!"
"Why not?" asked the gazelle.
"Well," said his mother.
"Gazelles are herbivores.
That means we eat plants.
But lions are carnivores.
They eat meat."
"Meat?" said the gazelle.
"Like other animals?"
"Yes," said his mother.
"The other day I saw a jackal eating berries," said the gazelle.
"Can I be friends with him?"
"No," said his mother.
"Jackals are omnivores.
They eat some plants.
But they also eat other animals."
"Meat eaters are terrible!" said the gazelle.
"No, they're not terrible," said his mother.
"That's just how the food chain works."
"Food chain?" asked the gazelle.
"Yes," said his mother.
"All living things need food for energy.
Plants get their energy from sunlight.
We get our energy from eating plants.
And meat eaters get it from eating other animals."
"I guess I understand," said the gazelle.
"Too bad that lion is a meat eater.
We had so much fun."
My garden has many visitors.
I say hello to them.
The snail takes his shell everywhere.
"Hello, Mr. Snail."
The caterpillar chews on a leaf.
"Hello, Mrs. Caterpillar."
The ant takes some food to his family.
"Hello, Mr. Ant."
The spider hangs from her web.
"Hello, Mrs. Spider."
The ladybug crawls on the bush.
"Hello, Mrs. Ladybug."
The bees buzz around the flowers.
"Hello, Mr. and Mrs. Bee."
I like all the visitors in my garden.
[g@Mom opened the car door.
"Cassie, meet Max.
He's our new pet."@g]
Cassie grinned as a black dog ran toward her.
[g@The dog wagged his tail and licked her face.
Then he jumped into her lap.@g]
"He likes you," Mom said.
[g@"I like him too," Cassie said.
"I'm going to take him everywhere!"@g]
The next day Mom and Cassie took Max downtown.
They went to the library first.
[g@"I'm sorry," the librarian said.
"No dogs are allowed in the library."@g]
Next they went to the pharmacy.
"Ugh." Cassie groaned when she saw the sign on the window.
"No Dogs Allowed."
After the pharmacy, they walked to the butcher shop.
[g@The butcher glared at them.
"No dogs are allowed!" he said.@g]
While Mom bought some meat for dinner, Cassie waited outside.
"I wanted to take you everywhere, Max," she said sadly.
"But everyone says, 'No dogs are allowed!'"
Max looked up and licked her face.
"Let's walk home through the park," Mom said.
Suddenly Max sniffed the air.
"I think he wants us to follow him," Cassie said.
[g@Max ran through the park.
Cassie heard loud barking.@g]
Then Max stopped near a tall fence.
[g@Cassie read the sign on the gate:
Friendly Dogs Welcome.@g]
[g@"Yay! It's a dog park!" she cried.
"Dogs are welcome here!"@g]
She bent down to hug her new pet.
"I guess I can't take you everywhere, Max.
But we can always come here together!"
"Woof!" Max barked happily.
[g@Can you guess who I am?
I am a blue whale.
Am I a fish? No!@g]
[g@A fish is born from an egg, but I am not.
I am a mammal!@g]
A fish can breathe under the water, but I cannot.
So, I have to come out of the water to breathe.
[g@Look at me breathe!
I spout water high into the air.@g]
[g@I am the biggest of all living animals.
I am longer than five buses.@g]
[g@I am the heaviest kind of whale.
I weigh more than twenty elephants.@g]
[g@But I can dive very deep.
Then, I can quickly swim back up again.@g]
You think I eat the largest fish, don't you?
[g@No, I just eat the smallest creatures in the ocean.
They are called plankton.@g]
[g@I also eat krill.
I like krill the best.@g]
[g@I have no teeth.
I just have a row of 320 plates.@g]
[g@The plates help me catch my food.
Let me show you how I eat.@g]
First, I gulp a large mouthful of water.
Then, I push the water out of my mouth.
Finally, I lick the small creatures off my plates with my huge tongue.
I am an amazing creature! Ha-ha!
[g@When you sail on the ocean, wave at me.
Then, I will salute you!@g]
Over in the meadow, in the sand in the sun,
Lived an old mother toad and her little toadie one.
"Wink!" said the mother.
"I wink!" said the one.
So they winked and they blinked in the sand in the sun.
Over in the meadow, where the stream runs blue,
Lived an old mother fish and her little fishes two.
"Swim!" said the mother.
"We swim!" said the two.
So they swam and they leaped where the stream runs blue.
Over in the meadow, in a hole in a tree,
Lived an old mother bluebird and her little birdies three.
"Sing!" said the mother.
"We sing!" said the three.
So they sang and were glad in a hole in the tree.
Over in the meadow, in the reeds on the shore,
Lived an old mother muskrat and her little ratties four.
"Dive!" said the mother.
"We dive!" said the four.
So they dived and they burrowed in the reeds on the shore.
Over in the meadow, in a snug beehive,
Lived a mother honey bee and her little bees five.
"Buzz!" said the mother.
"We buzz!" said the five.
So they buzzed and they hummed in the snug beehive.
Over in the meadow, in a nest built of sticks,
Lived a black mother crow and her little crows six.
"Caw!" said the mother.
"We caw!" said the six.
So they cawed and they called in their nest built of sticks.
Over in the meadow, where the grass is so even,
Lived a gay mother cricket and her little crickets seven.
"Chirp!" said the mother.
"We chirp!" said the seven.
So they chirped cheery notes in the grass soft and even.
Over in the meadow, by the old mossy gate,
Lived a brown mother lizard and her little lizards eight.
"Bask!" said the mother.
"We bask!" said the eight.
So they basked in the sun by the old mossy gate.
Over in the meadow, where the quiet pools shine,
Lived a green mother frog and her little froggies nine.
"Croak!" said the mother.
"We croak!" said the nine.
So they croaked and they splashed where the quiet pools shine.
Over in the meadow, in a sly little den,
Lived a gray mother spider and her little spiders ten.
"Spin!" said the mother.
"We spin!" said the ten.
So they spun lacy webs in their sly little den.
Oh, what time is it?
Is Nancy up already?
No, she isn't.
"Woof! Woof! Nancy! Nancy!
Time to get up!"
"Okay! Okay! I am getting up."
Every morning, I must wake her up.
It is fun to watch Nancy brush her teeth.
"Woof! Woof! Time to get dressed!"
Nancy puts on a skirt.
Nancy pulls on socks too.
"Muffy! Where is my schoolbag?"
"What?"
Nancy looks in her closet.
I look under the desk.
I find her bag under the desk. "Woof! Woof!"
"Woof! Woof! Time to eat now!"
Nancy eats a piece of toast.
I eat my breakfast too.
"Hurry! Here comes the school bus! Woof! Woof!"
"Woof! Woof! Nancy!
Don't forget your cap!"
Whew! She always forgets something!
But my job is not done yet.
I must clean up her mess.
Hmm. But I am a bit sleepy now.
I will take a nap.
I need to rest until Nancy comes back.
Hello! I am a baby elephant.
When I was only three days old, I began to walk.
I like to eat all kinds of plants.
[g@I like to eat fruit and bark too.
But I do not eat meat.@g]
[g@Let me show you how I eat.
I use my long trunk to pick up food.@g]
I use my trunk to breathe and smell too.
I use my trunk to spray water on my body.
I can take a bath using my trunk! [i@Splash!@i]
[g@I use my trunk to throw dust all over my body.
Doesn't it look fun?@g]
[g@There is another kind of bath I like too.
I like to take a mud bath.@g]
Rolling in the mud is fun! Whee!
[g@Oh! It is so hot today.
I can flap my large ears to cool off my body. Ahh!@g]
I also flap my ears to chase the flies away. Shoo!
I can do so many things with my ears and trunk!
But there is one thing I cannot do. Jump!
The elephant is the only mammal that cannot jump.
[g@But that's okay.
I can walk faster than people!@g]
[g@Do you see my dad?
He has something I don't have yet.
Look at his tusks!@g]
[g@I wish I had huge tusks like my dad.
I think they look wonderful.@g]
Dad says that someday I will have huge tusks too.
[g@But I will have to wait.
When I grow up, I will look just like him!@g]
Sammy was a cute sparrow.
He flew over the river with his mom.
"Oh, Mom, it's cloudy today," Sammy said.
[g@"Yes, Sammy," said Mom.
"It looks like it will rain soon."@g]
"Mom, I'm hungry," Sammy complained.
[g@"Yes, I'm also hungry.
Let's find something to eat."@g]
"Mom, Mom!" Sammy said.
[g@"Rest in the woods.
I will go and get some food."@g]
"Can you do it by yourself?" Mom asked.
"Sure, I can!" Sammy was old enough to find food on his own.
He was a good flier too.
He flew around the river to look for insects.
[g@But he couldn't find a single one.
"Hmm, this is strange.@g]
Why can't I find any insects?" he wondered.
Sammy felt tired and went back to his mom.
"Mom, I searched hard, but I couldn't find a single insect.
I used to see insects everywhere, but now they are gone."
"Sammy, why don't you fly low?" Mom suggested.
"What? You want me to fly low?" Sammy asked.
[g@"Yes, fly low.
Then you will see the insects."@g]
[g@Sammy took his mom's advice.
He flew around the river again.@g]
This time he flew low.
"Wow! I couldn't find a single one when I flew high," he said.
"Now I can see many insects. Yay!"
Sammy caught a big insect and brought it to his mom.
"Mom, I don't understand.
Why are all the insects so close to the ground?"
His mother explained.
"Before it rains, the air gets moist.
The moisture in the air makes insects' wings heavy.
So the insects fly in the grass and bushes near the ground."
Sammy understood. "I get it!
So when it looks like it will rain, I should fly low to look for insects."
"Right!" said Mom.
Just then it started to rain.
Sammy and his mom watched the raindrops and smiled.
